        return "Workspace previously optimized for high-throughput API arrays."

Future Scope

Expanding this framework involves integrating secure, decentralized storage nodes or real-time relational maps. Ensuring chronological priority alongside semantic distance sorting will help the memory agent ignore deprecated codebase files while keeping primary operational parameters highly accessible.

title: LLM Interview Questions in 2026: 6 Debugging Scenarios and How to Answer Them
description:
Some applied LLM interviews skip "explain temperature" and start from a production symptom: answers are cut off, the bill doubled, behavior changed overnight. The answer shape that works: name the likely causes, say how you'd tell them apart, then say what you'd change.

Six of the 15 scenarios from the full guide, condensed:

1. A fact in the middle of a long prompt gets ignored

Name the effect: the "Lost in the Middle" study (Liu et al., 2023) found performance is often highest when relevant information sits at the beginning or end of the context and degrades when it's in the middle. Reproduce it by moving the fact to the edges. The fix is less context: fewer, better passages, the most relevant ones at the edges, and the question restated after long documents.

2. Answers are cut off, but only in production

Read the stop reason before guessing. OpenAI's finish_reason is length when the token limit was reached, and Anthropic's stop_reason is max_tokens. "Only in production" points to longer real inputs, a lower limit in the prod config, or a stop sequence that appears in real text. With reasoning models the cap includes reasoning tokens, so it can be hit before any visible output.

3. About 2% of structured responses fail to parse

Triage before fixing. Sort failures into buckets: truncated JSON (check the stop reason), valid JSON with the wrong shape, extra prose around the JSON, or a refusal. Each has a different fix: a bigger limit, schema-constrained output or one repair retry, or a separate refusal path. Count the buckets before and after each change so you know which fix moved the 2%.

4. The bill doubled, and traffic didn't

Break cost into requests × tokens per request × price, by endpoint and model; one of those moved. Usual suspects: a retry loop, an agent calling tools more often, a prompt or context that grew, chat history no longer trimmed, traffic routed to a pricier model, or prompt-cache reads that fell. Then add budgets: alerts on tokens per request and a cap on agent steps.

5. The prompt cache hit rate dropped to near zero after a deploy

Caching works on an exact prefix. Anthropic's docs say cache hits require 100 percent identical prompt segments, built in the order tools, system, messages, and a change at one level invalidates everything after it. Diff the prompt: a timestamp or user name moved into the system prompt, or tools reordered, is the classic cause. Also check timing, because the default cache lifetime is 5 minutes, so a quiet endpoint can miss even with an unchanged prefix.

6. Behavior changed overnight, and nothing was deployed

List what isn't in your deploy: the model behind the ID you call, retrieved data, upstream tools and the traffic itself. Check whether you call an alias or a pinned snapshot, rerun your eval set and compare with the last stored run. Prevention: pin model versions, run evals on a schedule, and log the model version returned with each response.

The pattern

Every scenario rewards the same habit: find a signal that separates the causes (stop reason, chunk timestamp, cache-read tokens, per-request cost) before changing anything. If you can say what you'd log so the next incident takes minutes, you're answering at the mid-to-senior level.

All 15 scenarios, with levels, follow-ups and links to the vendor docs: LLM Interview Questions (2026) on StackChief.

This post was written with the help of AI, as a summary of the StackChief article above.

title: How to Run a Fair 30-Minute Live Coding Interview
description:
Most live coding interviews test how well someone performs under pressure, not how well they code. A short, structured round fixes most of that, and gives you a better signal in less time.

The 30-minute structure

Time What happens
0–5 min Explain the problem, let the candidate ask questions
5–20 min Candidate codes, runs and tests
20–27 min Follow-up questions on their solution
27–30 min Candidate asks you questions

1. Pick a small, realistic problem

Skip puzzles. Choose something close to the real job: parse a log file, paginate an API response, fix a buggy function. It should be solvable in 15 minutes by someone good.

2. Let them use a real environment

Let candidates run code and look things up the way they would at work. Remembering syntax isn't the skill you're hiring for.

3. Spend the most effort on follow-ups

The solution tells you what. The follow-ups tell you why:

  • Why did you choose this approach?
  • What breaks if the input is 100x larger?
  • What edge case aren't you handling yet?
  • What would you change before shipping?

Follow-ups are also the hardest part to fake with memorised or AI-generated answers.

4. Score against one rubric

Score Meaning
1 Can't explain their own code
2 Explains what, not why
3 Explains why and names a trade-off
4 Compares options and adapts when the constraint changes

Write evidence, not adjectives. Free template: technical interview rubric.

5. Keep it consistent

Same problem, same time limit and same follow-ups for every candidate in the role. That's what makes it fair, and comparable.

Common mistakes

  • Problems that need a trick to solve
  • Silent interviewers (talk with the candidate)
  • Penalising a candidate for looking something up
  • Deciding in the first 5 minutes

Scaling it

If you're hiring several engineers, running this for every candidate takes a lot of senior time. Some teams use conversational AI interviews for the first round. The AI runs live coding with follow-up questions, saves a full transcript, and your engineers review it and run the final round.

More follow-up ideas: 30 technical interview follow-up questions

title: Handoff Note: Multi-Agent Systems Fail at the Seams
description:
Cross-post of Insights #12 — canonical: https://sheikhwasim.com/insights/handoff-note-agents-fail-at-the-seams/

Every agent in the pipeline passed its own evals. The claim still came out wrong.

When you split work across agents (a planner, an extractor, a reviewer), you add something no single-agent eval covers: the handoff. Each agent does its part well, and the system still loses the one fact that mattered, because nobody owned the space between them.

Most multi-agent bugs I review aren't model bugs. They're seam bugs. The fix is boring and it works: every agent passes a Handoff Note, a small typed record of what it knows, what it was told not to do, what's still open, and where each fact came from. The next agent reads the note first, and the system checks the note at every seam.

Quick use case

Situation. A regional insurer's claims intake team runs three agents. An intake agent reads the customer's email and attachments. An extractor pulls policy number, loss date, amount, and coverage type into the claims system. A reviewer agent checks the result and either approves it for an adjuster or kicks it back. Each agent has its own eval set, and each one scores well.

What broke. A customer wrote, "the water damage started before I renewed, but the agent on the phone said the old policy covers it." The intake agent caught it and summarized the case in a free-text paragraph. The extractor only took structured fields from the attachments, so it filed the claim under the new policy's dates. The reviewer re-read the attachments from scratch, saw consistent fields, and approved. The phone-call exception never reached the adjuster, and the claim was denied on a date technicality that took two weeks and an escalation to unwind.

No agent was "wrong" on its own test. The fact died in a paragraph that the next agent never had to read.

The fix (Handoff Note).

  1. Typed note, not prose. Each agent writes four lists: facts, constraints, open questions, and sources.
  2. Read the note before the raw input. The extractor starts from the intake note, so "possible prior-policy coverage" arrives as an open question it has to resolve or carry forward.
  3. Open questions can't disappear. A question is either answered with a source or passed on. The reviewer can't approve while one is still open.
  4. Check the seam. A cheap validator compares the note going in with the note coming out and flags any fact or question that vanished.
  5. Log the notes with the trace. When a claim goes wrong, you can see exactly which seam dropped what.

Same agents, same models. The exception now shows up on the adjuster's screen as an open question with the customer's own words attached.

Why per-agent evals aren't enough

Per-agent evals test each agent on its own input. In production, an agent's real input is the previous agent's output, and that output drifts as prompts, models, and upstream agents change. An extractor that's 98% accurate on clean attachments tells you nothing about whether it respects a caveat the intake agent raised.

Free-text summaries make this worse. They read well to humans and pass vibe checks, but they let the next agent pick what it pays attention to. Anything without a slot is optional, and optional facts get dropped under pressure.

The Handoff Note (five layers)

1. Four slots, always

Facts (with values), constraints ("don't file under the new policy until coverage is confirmed"), open questions, and sources (document, line, message ID). Keep it short. If a slot is empty, it says so on purpose.

2. Note first, raw input second

The receiving agent's prompt starts with the note and treats it as the brief. It can still read the raw documents, but it has to reconcile anything that conflicts with the note instead of quietly overwriting it.

3. Questions are conserved

An open question leaves a seam in one of two states: answered, with a source, or still open. "Gone" isn't a state. This one rule catches most dropped-exception bugs.

4. A boring validator at every seam

Not another LLM judge, just code. Diff the incoming and outgoing notes. Missing facts, missing questions, or new facts with no source fail the handoff and route to a human or a retry. This is the Boundary Contract idea applied between agents instead of between an agent and a tool.

5. Notes live in the trace

Store every note with the run, stamped with the Release Pin. When something goes wrong, you can replay the seams instead of guessing which agent "probably" missed it, and you can turn the bad run into a Golden Trace for the whole pipeline.

How this maps to what you already have

  • 5-layer agent stack. The note is the contract between Orchestration and each agent's Memory, and it's recorded in Traces.
  • Golden Trace. Add pipeline-level golden runs that assert which facts and questions survive end to end.
  • Shadow Path. When you swap one agent in the chain, shadow it and compare its outgoing notes, not just its final labels.
  • Ship Gate. Add one check: no seam in the pipeline accepts free-text-only handoffs.

A test you can run this week

Take ten recent runs of any multi-agent flow. For each one, list every caveat, exception, or "but" in the original input. Then check whether each one is visible in the final output or explicitly resolved somewhere along the way.

If even one disappeared without a trace, you have a seam bug. Add the four-slot note at that seam before you touch a prompt or a model.

Closing

Agents don't usually fail alone. They fail at the handoff, where a fact one agent knew never became something the next agent had to deal with. Give every seam a typed note, conserve open questions, check the diff with plain code, and keep the notes in the trace. Make the handoff the part you can audit.

title: BI MCP or Warehouse MCP? A 7-toggle rubric for picking the right doorway
description:
One question I keep getting as a BI MCP builder serving a large enterprise user base: which MCP should I use for this use case?

Not "which one is better." Which doorway for this job.

The question usually arrives in a stronger form: "Why do we need a BI MCP when the warehouse MCP does the job?" The lazy answer is "because BI has a semantic layer." That's true and useless. It doesn't tell a team which doorway to give their agent on Monday.

I got tired of answering it from scratch every time, so I turned the answer into seven toggles. Here they are — and there's an interactive version at the end that gives you the verdict.

The 7 questions

1. Who's asking?
Others — stakeholders, customers, anyone non-technical → BI MCP. They can't validate raw SQL; they need answers built from vetted definitions.
You, and you know the data → warehouse MCP. A data engineer asking for themselves can read the SQL, spot a bad join, re-ask. No curation needed.

2. Does it need a defined business metric?
Yes — "revenue," "churn," "active user" → BI MCP. If two people can define the term differently, the definition must come from the model, not the model's imagination.
No — row counts, null rates, "what's in this table" → warehouse MCP. No business definition at stake; raw SQL is the honest tool.

3. One-off or repeated?
Repeated — dashboards, weekly reports → BI MCP. Repeated questions deserve a curated path: same definition, same shape, every time.
One-off — debugging, "let me check something" → warehouse MCP. Ad-hoc work dies in curation queues.

4. Do the consumers have warehouse access?
No → BI MCP, and this one is decisive. It's the only doorway that works. The BI tool queries under its own service identity while the end user has zero warehouse access; authorization happens at the BI project level. This is not a security hole — it's how BI works. The semantic layer is the authorization boundary.
Yes → either. Through the warehouse MCP the agent acts with the requester's own grants.

5. Exploring or asking a known question?
Exploring a new table, "what's possible here" → warehouse MCP. The curated model can't answer questions it wasn't built for.
Known business question → BI MCP.

6. Does the agent need to write or create?
Yes — DDL, staging tables, "build me a mart" → warehouse MCP. Decisive. The BI doorway is read-only by design.
No → either.

7. Does the semantic model cover this?
No → warehouse MCP, or go model it first. The honest caveat the semantic-layer pitch skips: BI MCP is only as good as the model behind it. An unmodeled question through the BI doorway gets a confident wrong answer or no answer.

The decision rule

Two of these are decisive: no warehouse access → BI MCP; needs writes → warehouse MCP. Otherwise, majority wins. A tie means hybrid — explore in the warehouse MCP, operationalize the metric in the semantic layer, serve it through BI MCP.

"Warehouse MCP" covers BigQuery, Snowflake, Databricks, Fabric. "BI MCP" covers Looker, dbt, Cube — any semantic-layer doorway.

Try it

I built the rubric as an interactive page — seven toggles, live verdict:
https://sangaraju1988.github.io/mcp-doorway-rubric/

And the repo (CC BY 4.0 — use it, credit it):
https://github.com/sangaraju1988/mcp-doorway-rubric

Two caveats

Managed warehouse MCP endpoints ship with guardrails — row caps, runtime caps. They rarely bind for aggregated Q&A, but bulk extraction belongs to the warehouse API, not any MCP doorway.

And unguarded agent + raw warehouse = surprise bills. Cost guardrails (quotas, dry runs, billed-bytes limits) belong in the warehouse MCP setup.

Most mature teams end up running both doorways. The rubric just tells you which one for this job.

title: Who controls how your agents use models?
description:
Post 1 of 8 in the GenAI gateway series.

The first agent is easy. You pick a model, give the agent credentials, connect its tools, and test the result. You know which model it calls and where to look when something goes wrong.

Then another team builds an agent on a different model. A third team joins. Each agent works, but a month later someone forwards the model bill and asks a short question nobody can answer: which of these agents spent this?

Other questions follow. Which agents can use the most expensive model? What data can they send? Who checks that the organisation's rules apply to every team?

Customers ask me some version of this all the time. Before this series, I deployed a governed agentic platform from an empty AWS account, and one piece of it kept coming up in every conversation: the layer that every model call passes through. So I spent the last two weeks deploying a gateway privately on AWS, testing each feature, and keeping notes on what broke. This series is those notes.

It starts with questions, because they explain why a gateway earns a place in an agent platform. Try answering the ones below for your own setup.

The setup that creates the questions

Picture ten agents across four teams: a support agent, an incident investigator, a code reviewer, a release checker and an inventory analyst. Between them they call five models, chosen for different tasks and costs.

Each agent talks to its model directly. Each team wrote its own client code, picked its own retry settings, and decided for itself what counts as a safe prompt.

One task is rarely one model call. An incident investigator asks a model what to check, calls a tool, sends the result back, and decides whether to dig further. A retry or a loop adds more calls. Whatever rules you have must cover the whole sequence.

Every team's choices make sense on their own. Look across all ten agents and new jobs appear that no single team owns: access, spending, data policy, reliability and visibility.

I hit this early in my own lab. I had one test team in the gateway. When I added a second team for a workload agent, I had to decide its budget, its rate limit and the two models it could call. The gateway gave me one place to configure those controls for both teams.

The questions

Who is allowed to call what?

  • Which agent can call which model? Is that written down anywhere, or is it whatever the credentials happen to allow?
  • When a new agent needs a model, what do you hand it? If the answer is cloud credentials, how narrow are they?
  • One agent's credentials leak. Can you revoke that agent alone, without breaking the other nine?
  • Does an experimental agent have the same model access as your production support agent?

Access defined in ten places is understood in none.

Who spent the money?

  • Suppose the bill went up 40% last month. Which agent, which team, which model caused it?
  • An agent gets stuck in a loop at 2 a.m. and keeps calling your largest model. What stops it?
  • Can you give one team a monthly budget and have it enforced, not just reported after the fact?
  • Do you know the per-token price of every model you use? Who updates it when prices change?

A budget you only read at month end is a receipt, not a limit.

Where are the organisation's data and content rules applied?

  • A tool returns output with instructions that try to redirect the agent. What checks it before the next model call?
  • A tool returns customer details or an access key. Can those values reach the model, and which policy decides?
  • Do all ten agents apply the same content policy? Who would notice if one didn't?
  • When the policy changes, how many codebases need a release?

If you can't verify that a check ran, you can't rely on it.

What happens when a model has a bad day?

  • A model starts throttling. Does each agent retry, fail, or hang?
  • Is there a backup model? Has anyone tested whether the agent still completes its task with it?
  • A model version is retired. How many agents break, and how do you find them?

A fallback that returns an answer your agent can't use isn't a fallback.

Can you see what's happening?

  • Can you trace yesterday's model calls to an agent, a team and a task, with latency, token usage and estimated cost?
  • An agent made a poor decision last Tuesday. Can you find the calls behind it, within what your data policy lets you keep?
  • A task took too long. How much of that was model calls, and where do you look for the rest?

Model logs that don't line up with the agent's own trace give you pieces of a task, not the task.

How fast can you change models?

  • A cheaper model ships that's good enough for half your agents. How many code changes does it take to move them?
  • Someone wants to try an open-weight model for a week. How long before they can?
  • By the end of my lab, my gateway listed more than 80 models. Picture granting ten agents access to that list one codebase at a time.

A shared model name turns a code change into a config change. It doesn't remove the need to test each agent on the new model.

Are you paying for the same answer twice?

  • How many of today's model requests repeat an earlier one, and which responses are safe to reuse?
  • Your agents send the same long system prompt with every call. Are you paying full price for it every time?

A shared view makes it easier to spot repeated requests across agents. And a cached answer is only safe if it's right for the agent asking and the data hasn't changed.

The shape of every answer

Every question here is a decision that spans teams: who can use a model, what they can send, how much they can spend, and what happens when a call fails. Leave each decision inside each agent and you maintain ten versions of the same control.

That is why agents need a gateway: one service between them and every model they call.

Configure it, and the gateway becomes the one place where model access is checked, usage is attributed, budgets and rate limits apply, inputs and outputs are screened, and retries and fallbacks follow one policy. Agents call one interface, and every call is recorded the same way.

Teams still own their agents' reasoning, tools and results. The platform owner owns the controls on the model call.

What a gateway doesn't answer

A gateway only governs traffic that goes through it. Until agents lose direct access to models, it's a suggestion, not a control.

It also doesn't decide whether an agent may run a tool, change a record or act on an answer. A budget on model calls doesn't limit what the agent does between them. Screening a prompt doesn't guarantee the agent resists every injection attempt.

And it's a service to run. Someone has to secure it, monitor it and plan for it failing, because every agent depends on it. The next post covers that work.

What to take from this

  • Agent count isn't the test. The test is whether you can enforce your rules on model calls and show that you did.
  • One production agent can justify a gateway. The case gets stronger when several teams need shared controls over model access and spending.
  • List the access, spending and data rules that must hold across every agent. Those are the gateway's job. Give it an owner.

Your agents differ in almost everything except the model call. That's where the shared rules belong.

Next in the series: deploying the gateway on AWS.

title: [Boost]

title: How Renaming Sam Altman to "RAM Altman" Saved Our Production Server (And Why Hard-Altman Is Next)
description:
It was 3:15 AM on a Tuesday. The monitoring dashboards were glowing with the unmistakable crimson of catastrophic failure. Memory Usage was pinned at 99.8%. In the dark, silent corridors of our Linux kernel, the Out-of-Memory (OOM) Killer was roaming free—execution-style terminating background workers, Redis instances, and anything that dared to consume more than a few megabytes.
Then came the push notification that changed everything.
Amidst global supply chain panics and skyrocketing cloud infrastructure bills, Sam Altman—the face of modern AI—silently updated his profile name on X (Twitter) to "Ram Altman".
Naturally, in my sleep-deprived state, I had only one logical thought: If changing a name can address a global hardware shortage, can we solve our memory leaks by renaming our architecture?
The Root Cause: Modern Software Engineering
Before we attempt to patch our servers with raw cope, we must face the uncomfortable truth of how we got here:
[ Your Application ]
│
├──► 450 MB: Node.js runtime
├──► 800 MB: 1,400 npm packages (to pad a string)
├──► 1.2 GB: Chromium (running headless for "logging")
└──► 12 KB: Actual business logic

We used to write software that ran on 64 KB of RAM and put humans on the Moon. Today, we ship a 600 MB Electron app just so users can check a todo list. When production runs out of memory, our first instinct isn't to profile heap allocation or fix memory leaks—it’s to slide the RAM slider on AWS to the right and hand over our department’s budget to Andy Jassy.
Phase 1: Psychological Patching (altman.patch)
If Sam Altman can pivot to RAM, our codebase can adapt too. We created a hotfix script designed to trick the OS into thinking our heap size was boundless through sheer linguistic persuasion:

!/bin/bash

Emergency OOM Mitigation Script v1.0.4

echo "Applying Ram-Altman-Protocol..."

Search for all instances of "Sam" and upgrade to "Ram"

find ./src -type f ( -name ".js" -o -name ".ts" ) -exec sed -i 's/Sam/Ram/g' {} +

Alias garbage collector to sound more optimistic

alias node="node --max-old-space-size=65536 --optimize-for-size"

echo "System successfully rebranded. Good luck."

Result: The OOM Killer remained entirely unbothered by our semantic humor and promptly wiped out our main PostgreSQL process anyway.
Phase 2: Fan theories on the "RAM Altman" Shift
Why did the change actually happen? As engineers, we must formulate hypotheses:

  • The LLM Memory Wall: OpenAI’s next-gen models have scaled so far that context windows are no longer measured in tokens, but in raw Terabytes of RAM per request.
  • Hardware Arbitrage: He bought out the global DDR5 supply chain to train GPT-6, leaving the rest of us fighting over secondhand 4GB SODIMMs on eBay.
  • The Ultimate Irony: He’s subtly reminding the dev community that no matter how advanced your neural networks are, they still run on physical silicon that chokes when you forget to close your database connections. The Hard Truth: No Rebrand Will Fix Bad Code As funny as it was watching the tech universe react to "RAM Altman" for a day, the takeaway for developers is surprisingly grounded: You cannot scale out of terrible architecture forever. We’ve spent the last decade using hardware abstraction layers to cover up lazy code. We import entire frameworks to use a single utility function. We ignore memory leaks because "cloud RAM is cheap"—until the invoice arrives, or until the hardware market squeezes. Until we start respecting hardware limits, writing lean routines, and profiling our applications before deployment, no amount of cloud budget—and no Twitter rebrand—is going to save our servers. What’s your worst OOM emergency story? Drop your wildest memory leak war stories in the comments below! Created by : https://almodarresieh.github.io/

title: AI Token Black Market: How Stolen API Keys Are Resold
description:
The AI token black market turns a leaked key into inventory. You check your cloud dashboard on a Monday and the bill for your AI project is 40 times higher than last week. Nobody shipped anything big. No traffic spike. Just a steady burn of tokens you never used.

That scenario shows up in incident reports often enough now that security teams treat it as routine. Through 2026, researchers and AI labs documented a working underground economy around one asset: AI API keys. Criminals steal them, wrap them in cheap resellers, and sell access to anyone who wants frontier models at a discount. The account owner pays.

This guide walks through the pipeline, the evidence, and the controls that actually reduce your risk. It also covers the buyer's side, because a cheap endpoint can cost you more than money.

What the AI token black market actually sells

A token is the unit of text a large language model reads and writes. Providers bill per token, and access is gated by an API key, a long secret string that behaves like a password with a credit card attached.

Demand for cheap frontier access is real. So is the supply chain that formed around it. Three tiers get mixed together in most conversations, so keep them apart:

Tier What it is Legal status Main risk to you
Legitimate gateway An open-source router a team runs with its own paid keys Legal Misconfiguration
Gray-market relay Resellers pooling accounts, trial credits or discounted capacity against provider terms Often violates terms of service Swapped models, data exposure
Black market Resale of stolen keys, hijacked accounts and fraudulent proxies Illegal Account bans, legal exposure, malware

The vocabulary around this space is a mess. Here is the short version.

  • LLMjacking: using stolen credentials to run model workloads on someone else's account.
  • Token jacking: Unit 42's term for hijacking stolen AI access tokens and routing them to gray-market resellers.
  • Transfer stations: reseller platforms, common in the Chinese-language ecosystem, that proxy requests to official APIs at rock-bottom prices.
  • Shadow APIs: third-party services that claim to offer an official model and may serve something else.
  • Distillation: training a cheaper model on a stronger model's outputs, one reason some actors want bulk tokens.

How a stolen key becomes a resale service

The pipeline reported by Cybernews, VentureBeat, Anthropic's September 2026 threat intelligence report and independent researchers looks much the same each time.

flowchart TD
    A["Key leaks<br/>repos, apps, containers, malware"] --> B["Scanner validates<br/>and pools live keys"]
    B --> F["Attacker strips<br/>spend limits and logging"]
    B --> C["Relay or transfer station<br/>looks like a normal API"]
    C --> D["Buyers pay 70-90% below list"]
    D --> E["Victim's account pays the bill"]

Step 1: Harvest the keys

Anthropic's report puts customer mistakes at the top of the list. Keys end up in GitHub repositories, mobile app bundles, Docker images, websites and chatbot front ends.

Other documented sources:

  • Supply chain attacks. CloudSEK traced a package compromise that started in March 2026 and exposed cloud keys, repository tokens, SSH keys, Kubernetes secrets and AI provider keys across thousands of downstream projects. Cybernews links npm campaigns such as Shai-Hulud and Miasma to the same pool of stolen credentials.
  • Infostealer malware. One 2026 incident began with an employee at a major platform company opening an infected file. Attackers harvested workspace credentials and reached the API keys behind them.
  • Prompt injection against LLM gateways. Anthropic describes attackers tricking LiteLLM deployments into leaking the production credentials sitting behind them.
  • Compromised evaluation sandboxes. The same report covers keys from more than 30 AI companies stolen through one compromised sandbox.
  • Exposed self-hosted model servers. Misconfigured local servers open to the internet have also been hit.

Step 2: Validate and pool

Scanners crawl public code hosting, test each key, and move the live ones into pools. The window is short. A key pushed to a public repo can be found and tested in minutes.

Step 3: Wrap the keys in a relay

Raw keys are awkward to sell. Operators build a relay that looks like a normal API instead. A buyer gets an endpoint and a key of their own. Requests get proxied through stolen credentials behind it.

Researchers who studied this stack point to open-source gateways like one-api and new-api as the plumbing. Those tools are neutral and widely used by teams for quotas. The line gets crossed when the channels behind them hold stolen, leaked or trial-farmed keys.

Attackers also cover their tracks. Cybernews described them creating new keys on the compromised account, removing billing limits, and switching off usage alerts and logging.

Step 4: Sell the access

Sales run through Telegram channels, Discord servers, marketplaces and polished storefronts. VentureBeat described Telegram vendors offering 24/7 support and money-back guarantees, with one seller advertising several Claude models at once. Reported discounts sit between 70 and 93 percent below list.

Google threat intelligence, cited in the same reporting, shows more buyers and more sellers advertising AI accounts through 2026, with average prices per account more than doubling.

Why the prices look impossible

The seller usually did not pay for the compute. A few models explain the pricing:

  1. Stolen keys. Cost to the seller is close to zero. The victim's card gets charged.
  2. Trial farming. Mass-created free-tier accounts, with the credits pooled.
  3. Model substitution. A premium model in the listing, a cheaper one behind the endpoint.
  4. Data harvesting. Access sold at a loss because your prompts, source code and customer data are the product.

That fourth one matters if you paste private code into a mystery proxy. You just handed it to an unknown third party.

The evidence so far

Finding Source Why it matters
45.83% of tested shadow API endpoints failed model fingerprint verification; another 12.50% showed major identity deviations CISPA Helmholtz Center, "Real Money, Fake Models" (March 2026) A cheap endpoint often does not serve the model it names
At least 187 academic papers had used shadow APIs Same audit Some published results may rest on a substituted model
About 30 AI companies hit in roughly four days using victims' keys Anthropic threat report (September 10, 2026) Key theft is fast and automated
A hacktivist campaign ran for a month on stolen API keys Anthropic threat report Stolen keys fund attacks, not only free chatbots
Credential theft aimed at AI services reportedly grew 376% from Q4 2025 to Q1 2026 Industry write-up citing underground tracking Treat as directional, and verify against primary sources
Dark-web listings for some model keys reportedly start near $15 Secondary industry reporting Low prices are the lure, not a sign of legitimacy

Two of those are primary sources: the CISPA paper and Anthropic's report. Some pricing and growth figures come from secondary write-ups. Use them as context, not as hard numbers in your own documentation.

Who loses money, and who loses data

Developers and startups feel it first. A key without a spending limit can generate a serious bill within hours, and small teams have no finance department to absorb the shock.

Companies and their customers get hit twice. Attackers use stolen keys as attack compute, and legitimate users lose quota when it runs dry. Because the traffic looks like normal usage, detection is hard.

Buyers of cheap access are not safe either. You may get a weaker model, leaked prompts, an account ban when the key is revoked, or malware. Anthropic's report describes fraudulent resellers that proxied traffic to a different model while harvesting credentials from the customers who signed up. The buyer's own keys became inventory.

Researchers get bad data. The CISPA audit found accuracy on a medical benchmark dropped sharply for one shadow endpoint compared with the official model. If your evaluation ran through a swapped model, your results do not reproduce.

A practical API key security checklist

You do not need an enterprise team to cut most of this risk. Start with these.

1. Never hardcode keys

Keep secrets out of source files. Use environment variables or a secrets manager.

# .env (never commit this file)
OPENAI_API_KEY=your-key-here

# .gitignore
.env
.env.*

import os

api_key = os.environ.get("OPENAI_API_KEY")
if not api_key:
    raise RuntimeError("Missing API key. Set it in your environment.")

2. Scan before you commit

Add a secret scanner to your pre-commit hook and your CI pipeline.

gitleaks detect --source . --verbose

Deleting a key from the latest commit does not remove it from history. Rotate it.

3. Set spending limits and alerts

Most providers let you set monthly budgets and usage alerts. Turn them on and send alerts to a channel people read. Attackers try to disable these, so alert on changes to billing limits and key creation too.

4. Use scoped, short-lived keys

Create separate keys per project and per environment. Restrict each one to the models and endpoints it needs. Rotate on a schedule, and immediately after any staff change or suspected exposure.

5. Keep keys out of client code

Never ship a provider key in a mobile bundle, browser JavaScript or a public Docker image. Route requests through your own backend, which holds the key and enforces per-user rate limits.

6. Harden your LLM gateway

If you run LiteLLM or a similar proxy, do not expose it to the open internet without authentication. Patch it, restrict admin routes, and treat prompt injection as a real path to credential leakage. Give the gateway only the key access it needs.

7. Watch your dependencies

Pin versions, use lockfiles, review new packages and run dependency audits. Supply chain compromises are a major source of stolen environment variables. Our gh-secure setup walkthrough shows how to switch on secret scanning and push protection for a public repo in about two minutes.

8. Monitor usage like a production system

Look for unfamiliar models, odd hours, new regions, sudden token spikes and requests that do not match your app's patterns. Billing anomaly detection is often the first signal.

9. Buy through official channels

Anthropic's guidance is to buy AI access only from the provider directly, or through approved cloud marketplaces and verified partners.

How to spot a risky AI reseller

Run this table against any third-party gateway before you trust it.

Red flag Why it matters
Price is 70 to 90 percent below list Someone else is covering the difference
No company, no terms, no privacy policy You cannot know what happens to your prompts
Payment only in crypto or chat apps Hard to dispute, common in scams
"Unlimited" frontier model access Capacity is oversold or pooled
Asks for your own provider key to "cut costs" Your key may be harvested and resold
Model behavior differs from the official API Possible model substitution
Closed-source client you must install Malware or key exfiltration risk

If you have to evaluate an endpoint for research, do not trust the model name. Compare responses against the official API on a fixed prompt set, check token counts and latency, and run benchmark tasks with a known official score. The CISPA paper describes fingerprinting methods worth reading before you build your own.

If your key is already stolen

  1. Revoke the key in your provider dashboard.
  2. Check usage logs for the time window, models and IP ranges involved.
  3. Look for new keys and changed billing or logging settings. Attackers often create their own.
  4. Find the leak. Search repos, CI logs, container images, app bundles and recent dependency changes.
  5. Rotate other secrets that lived in the same place, including cloud keys and tokens.
  6. Contact provider support about disputed charges and share your timeline.
  7. Add the controls above so it does not happen twice.

The legal gray zone

Reselling your own legitimately purchased capacity in line with a provider's terms can be fine. Buying from a service that sells stolen keys is a different matter, and it can expose you to account termination and legal risk. Even gray-market pooling often breaks provider terms.

This article gives general information. For legal advice, read the terms of service for anything you use and talk to a lawyer before you build a business on a reseller.

Where this goes next

Expect more automation. Agents that read repos, call tools and spend money raise the stakes because the credentials they hold are powerful. Security teams are already arguing that AI keys and agent integrations belong in the same inventory as production credentials, with rotation, scoping and monitoring.

If you build with coding agents, how AI coding agents work explains the permission model, and OpenCode MCP servers covers the tool surface they reach. Our codebase auditor skill helps you catch exposed secrets earlier. And if cost is what pushed you toward a shady reseller, start with a legitimate free vibe coding setup instead.

Where the numbers come from

  • Cybernews, "Token theft now is an industry" (August 6, 2026)
  • VentureBeat, reporting on Anthropic's September 2026 threat intelligence report and underground account pricing
  • CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security, "Real Money, Fake Models: Deceptive Model Claims in Shadow APIs" (March 2026)
  • Business Standard, "Hackers target AI supply chains as stolen tokens fuel new cyber threat" (August 2026)
  • GitHub Docs, secret scanning

Key Takeaways

  • The AI token black market resells stolen or abused API keys, hijacked accounts and fraudulent proxies at deep discounts.
  • Most stolen keys leak from customers' own environments: public repos, app bundles, containers and compromised dependencies.
  • Resale usually runs through relays or transfer stations that proxy to official APIs after attackers remove spending limits and logging.
  • Cheap endpoints are risky for buyers too. A CISPA audit found that 45.83% of tested shadow API endpoints failed fingerprint checks.
  • If a price looks too good, assume someone else is paying for it.

Frequently asked questions

What is the black market for AI tokens?

An underground ecosystem where stolen API keys, hijacked accounts and fraudulent proxies are sold at steep discounts. Buyers get cheap model access while the legitimate account owner gets the bill.

How does the AI token black market work?

Attackers steal keys from exposed repositories, apps, containers, malware or supply chain attacks. They validate and pool the keys, wrap them in a relay that looks like a normal API, then sell access through Telegram, Discord or storefronts far below official rates.

Why are stolen AI API keys so valuable?

A key grants access to paid model quota that can be spent immediately and resold. Since the seller did not pay for the compute, they can undercut official prices and still profit. Keys for advanced models are in the highest demand.

What are transfer stations in the AI token market?

Reseller platforms that proxy requests to official AI APIs, often with stolen or pooled credentials, while advertising very low prices. The term is common in coverage of the Chinese-language reseller ecosystem.

How do stolen AI keys usually leak?

Anthropic's September 2026 report points to customer mistakes first: keys exposed in GitHub repos, mobile app files, Docker containers, websites and chatbots. Malware, supply chain attacks and prompt injection against LLM gateways are also documented.

How do I protect my AI API keys?

Store keys in environment variables or a secrets manager, scan repos before you commit, set spending limits and alerts, use scoped and rotating keys, keep keys out of client code, secure your LLM gateways, and watch usage for anomalies.

Conclusion

The economics are simple. Stolen compute is free for the seller and expensive for the victim, and a relay makes it easy to resell. Your defense is boring work: short-lived scoped keys, secret scanning, spending limits and a habit of watching usage.

For a design that removes provider keys from your app entirely, our guide to building a SaaS app with Puter.js walks through a keyless, user-pays setup.

If you want to write up what you find, our contributor guide explains how to submit. Every post here, including this one, is checked against the standards in our editorial policy.

title: Your AI agent will send that email twice. Here's how to stop it
description:
Give an AI agent a send_email tool and, sooner or later, a customer gets the same receipt twice.

Nothing is broken when it happens. Every piece works the way it was built to:

  • The HTTP call to your email API times out after 10 seconds. The email was actually accepted at second 9. Your tool returns an error, so the agent tries again.
  • The model sees a tool error and re-plans. Its second attempt rewrites the subject line "to be safe" and calls the tool again.
  • Your agent framework retries failed tool calls automatically. So does your HTTP client. So does the queue worker that runs the agent. Three layers of retries, none of them aware of the others.
  • A long-running agent loses its context, restarts the task from its notes, and finds "send confirmation to Ana" still on the to-do list.

Each of these is a reasonable design choice on its own. Together they turn "exactly once" into "at least once", and with email, "at least once" means your customer sees it twice. Unlike a duplicated database row, you can't delete a sent email.

This post is the pattern I use to make email sends safe for agents: idempotency keys derived from the event, a strict retry policy, narrow tools, and an undo window for anything that isn't transactional. The code uses the Cresca email API (I'm building it, so that's the one I know best), but every idea works with any email API that accepts an Idempotency-Key header.

Why "just hash the arguments" doesn't work

The first fix everyone reaches for is to hash the tool's arguments and use that as the idempotency key. Same arguments, same hash, so the API ignores the duplicate. Clean.

It breaks the moment the agent is involved:

// Attempt 1, written by the model
const attempt1 = { to: "ana@example.com", subject: "Your order #1042 is confirmed", html: "<p>Hi Ana, ..." };

// Attempt 2, after a timeout. The model "improved" it.
const attempt2 = { to: "ana@example.com", subject: "Order #1042 confirmed!", html: "<p>Hello Ana, ..." };

Different arguments, different hash, two emails. A language model almost never produces byte-identical output twice, and when it re-plans after an error it is actively trying to do something different.

Hashing also fails in the other direction. If Ana places two orders that produce the same text, the hash matches and the second confirmation is silently dropped.

The key has to identify the thing that happened in the world, not the request that describes it.

Rule 1: derive the key from the event

An idempotency key answers one question: which real-world event is this email about?

order-confirmation/1042
password-reset/7f3c9a      ← the id of this reset request, not of the user
invoice-paid/inv_2026_0042
weekly-digest/user_881/2026-W45

The pattern is <event>/<id>. Three properties matter:

  1. Stable across retries. Every attempt to send the confirmation for order 1042 produces the same key, whoever makes the attempt: your code, the framework or the model.
  2. New when the event is new. If Ana asks for a password reset twice, those are two reset requests with two ids, and she should get two emails. Key on the request id, not on her user id.
  3. Never time-based or random. Date.now() or a fresh UUID per attempt defeats the whole point, because each retry gets a new key.

With Cresca, a request with a key the API has already seen (with the same body, within 24 hours) returns the original response instead of sending again, and adds the header idempotent-replayed: true. Two other cases are worth knowing:

Situation Response
Same key, same body, within 24 hours The first response again, with idempotent-replayed: true. Nothing is sent.
Same key, different body 409 invalid_idempotent_request
Same key while the first request is still being processed 409 concurrent_idempotent_requests. Retry shortly.
More than 24 hours later The key has expired, and the request is treated as new.

That second row is exactly the "model rewrote the subject" case. You get a loud 409 instead of a quiet duplicate, which is what you want.

Rule 2: don't let the model write transactional email

That 409 is useful, but you should rarely see it, because the model shouldn't be composing the receipt in the first place.

For transactional email (receipts, resets, verification codes, alerts), give the agent a tool that takes ids, not content:

// tools.js. The shape the model sees. (Field names differ slightly between
// SDKs: some call the schema `parameters`, others `input_schema`.)
export const tools = [
  {
    name: "send_order_confirmation",
    description:
      "Send the order confirmation email for one order. Safe to call more than once: " +
      "the same order never gets two confirmations. Use only after the order is paid.",
    schema: {
      type: "object",
      properties: {
        order_id: { type: "string", description: "The order id, e.g. 1042" },
      },
      required: ["order_id"],
      additionalProperties: false,
    },
  },
];

Your code looks up the order, builds the email from a template and owns the key. The model decides whether and when to send; it never decides what the email says or how it's identified.

This does three things at once:

  • Idempotency stops depending on the model. The key comes from the order id, which your code controls.
  • Hallucinated content is impossible. The model can't invent a discount, a wrong total or a link to the wrong account, because it never writes the body.
  • The tool description can promise safety. "Safe to call more than once" is now true, and models do read tool descriptions. It reduces the nervous re-calling you see when a tool has failed before.

Rule 3: retry the right failures, and only those

Here's the send function behind that tool. It's plain Node 18+ with fetch, no SDK:

// send-email.js
const API = "https://api.cresca.xyz/api/v1";
const KEY = process.env.CRESCA_API_KEY; // a "sending access" key: it can send, nothing else

const sleep = (ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms));

export async function sendEmail(payload, { idempotencyKey, maxAttempts = 5 } = {}) {
  if (!idempotencyKey) throw new Error("idempotencyKey is required for every send");

  for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= maxAttempts; attempt++) {
    let res;
    try {
      res = await fetch(`${API}/emails`, {
        method: "POST",
        headers: {
          Authorization: `Bearer ${KEY}`,
          "Content-Type": "application/json",
          "Idempotency-Key": idempotencyKey,
        },
        body: JSON.stringify(payload),
        signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10_000),
      });
    } catch (err) {
      // Network error or timeout: the email may or may not have been accepted.
      // Retrying with the SAME key is safe, so this is exactly when to retry.
      if (attempt === maxAttempts) throw err;
      await sleep(backoff(attempt));
      continue;
    }

    if (res.ok) {
      const body = await res.json();
      return { id: body.id, replayed: res.headers.get("idempotent-replayed") === "true" };
    }

    const error = await res.json().catch(() => ({}));

    // In flight elsewhere (another retry layer got there first): wait and ask again.
    if (res.status === 409 && error.name === "concurrent_idempotent_requests") {
      await sleep(backoff(attempt));
      continue;
    }

    // Rate limited: the server tells us how long to wait.
    if (res.status === 429 && error.name === "rate_limit_exceeded") {
      const wait = Number(res.headers.get("retry-after") || 1) * 1000;
      await sleep(wait + jitter());
      continue;
    }

    // Server-side trouble: back off and retry.
    if (res.status >= 500) {
      if (attempt === maxAttempts) break;
      await sleep(backoff(attempt));
      continue;
    }

    // Everything else is a bug in the request, a used-up monthly quota, or a key
    // reused with a different body. Retrying can't fix any of them. Fail loudly.
    throw new Error(`Email not sent: ${res.status} ${error.name}: ${error.message}`);
  }

  throw new Error(`Email not sent after ${maxAttempts} attempts`);
}

const jitter = () => Math.floor(Math.random() * 250);
const backoff = (attempt) => Math.min(1000 * 2 ** (attempt - 1), 8000) + jitter(); // 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s

And the tool handler that ties it to the order:

// handlers.js
import { sendEmail } from "./send-email.js";
import { getOrder } from "./orders.js";

export async function send_order_confirmation({ order_id }) {
  const order = await getOrder(order_id);
  if (!order) return { ok: false, error: `No order ${order_id}` };
  if (order.status !== "paid") return { ok: false, error: `Order ${order_id} is not paid yet` };

  const result = await sendEmail(
    {
      from: "Acme <orders@mail.acme.com>",
      to: order.customerEmail,
      template: {
        id: "order-confirmation", // a published template, by alias
        variables: { NAME: order.customerName, ORDER_ID: order.id, TOTAL: order.totalFormatted },
      },
      tags: [{ name: "category", value: "order_confirmation" }],
    },
    { idempotencyKey: `order-confirmation/${order.id}` },
  );

  // Tell the model plainly what happened, including "you already did this".
  return result.replayed
    ? { ok: true, note: `Confirmation for order ${order.id} was already sent earlier (id ${result.id}). Nothing new was sent.` }
    : { ok: true, note: `Confirmation for order ${order.id} sent (id ${result.id}).` };
}

That last return matters more than it looks. When the agent calls the tool a second time, it gets a clear answer, "already sent earlier", instead of a generic success it might second-guess. A clear answer like that is what stops the retry loop at the model level: there's nothing left to fix.

Three details in the retry policy are deliberate:

  • Network errors and timeouts are retried. They're the dangerous case: the email might have gone out. The idempotency key is what makes retrying them safe.
  • retry-after is respected on 429. Retrying a rate limit immediately just burns your next request.
  • Other 4xx responses are never retried. A validation error or an exhausted quota will fail the same way every time, and a retry loop here is how you end up with a stuck agent and a page of logs.

Rule 4: give non-transactional email an undo window

Receipts are easy because the content is fixed. The hard case is the email the agent does compose: "draft a follow-up to everyone who attended Tuesday's webinar and send it."

You can't key that on an order id, and you probably don't want a model hitting "send" on a message to 300 people with no human in the loop. The pattern I like is to schedule instead of sending, then let a person cancel:

// The agent's "send" tool for composed email schedules 15 minutes ahead.
export async function send_followup({ to, subject, html, campaign_id }) {
  const sendAt = new Date(Date.now() + 15 * 60 * 1000).toISOString();

  const { id } = await sendEmail(
    { from: "Acme <hello@acme.com>", to, subject, html, scheduled_at: sendAt },
    { idempotencyKey: `followup/${campaign_id}/${to}` },
  );

  await notifyHuman(
    `The agent scheduled "${subject}" to ${to} at ${sendAt}. ` +
      `Cancel within 15 minutes: POST /emails/${id}/cancel`,
  );
  return { ok: true, note: `Scheduled for ${sendAt}. A human can cancel it before then.` };
}

Cresca accepts scheduled_at up to 30 days ahead, and POST /emails/:id/cancel works while an email is still scheduled or queued; once sending has started it returns 422. A canceled email doesn't count toward your monthly allowance, so a canceled mistake costs nothing.

Fifteen minutes is arbitrary. Pick a window that matches how fast someone on your team actually looks at notifications. The point is that the agent's action becomes reversible for a while, which is the property email normally lacks.

Rule 5: give the agent a key that can only send

The agent runs with whatever credentials you give its tools. For email, that should be a key that can send and nothing else.

Cresca's sending access keys can call POST /emails and POST /emails/batch, but can't read your email logs or change templates. Your undo-window tool needs a full-access key to cancel, so keep that on the human side, in the notification handler, not in the agent's tools.

The general rule: the agent's credentials should match the agent's job, not your admin's.

The same pattern in Python

If your agent runs on a Python stack, here's the core of send_email with httpx:

import os, random, time
import httpx

API = "https://api.cresca.xyz/api/v1"
HEADERS = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['CRESCA_API_KEY']}"}

def send_email(payload: dict, idempotency_key: str, max_attempts: int = 5) -> dict:
    for attempt in range(1, max_attempts + 1):
        try:
            res = httpx.post(
                f"{API}/emails",
                json=payload,
                headers={**HEADERS, "Idempotency-Key": idempotency_key},
                timeout=10,
            )
        except httpx.TransportError:
            if attempt == max_attempts:
                raise
            time.sleep(backoff(attempt))
            continue

        if res.is_success:
            return {"id": res.json()["id"], "replayed": res.headers.get("idempotent-replayed") == "true"}

        name = res.json().get("name", "")
        if res.status_code == 409 and name == "concurrent_idempotent_requests":
            time.sleep(backoff(attempt)); continue
        if res.status_code == 429 and name == "rate_limit_exceeded":
            time.sleep(float(res.headers.get("retry-after", 1)) + random.random() / 4); continue
        if res.status_code >= 500 and attempt < max_attempts:
            time.sleep(backoff(attempt)); continue

        raise RuntimeError(f"Email not sent: {res.status_code} {name}: {res.json().get('message')}")
    raise RuntimeError(f"Email not sent after {max_attempts} attempts")

def backoff(attempt: int) -> float:
    return min(2 ** (attempt - 1), 8) + random.random() / 4

How to test that it actually works

Don't trust the pattern until you've watched it refuse to send twice. Three tests worth automating:

1. The replay test. Call your tool twice in a row for the same order and assert one email:

const a = await send_order_confirmation({ order_id: "test-1042" });
const b = await send_order_confirmation({ order_id: "test-1042" });
assert(a.ok && b.ok);
assert(b.note.includes("already sent"));

2. The timeout test. Point sendEmail at a proxy that accepts the request, waits past your 10-second timeout, then lets it through. Your code sees a timeout and retries; you should still end up with one email and replayed: true on the retry.

3. The model test. Run the agent with a tool that fails the first call on purpose ("network error"), and log every tool call it makes after that. You're checking two things: that the model's retries land on the same key, and that the "already sent" note stops it from calling a third time.

The checklist

Before you hand an agent a tool that sends email:

  • Every send carries an idempotency key built from the event (<event>/<id>), never from time, randomness or a hash of model output.
  • Transactional tools take ids, and your code builds the content from templates.
  • The retry policy retries network errors, timeouts, 429 (after retry-after) and 5xx, and nothing else.
  • A replayed send returns a clear "already sent" result to the model.
  • Composed or bulk email is scheduled, not sent, with a cancel window a human can use.
  • The agent's key can send, and only send.
  • You've watched the replay, timeout and model tests pass.

None of this is new. Payment APIs have worked this way for years, because charging a card twice is the same kind of mistake as emailing someone twice: you can't take it back. What's new is that the thing calling your API is now a model that retries creatively. Design the tool so that creativity can't cost your customer a duplicate email.

I'm building Cresca, an email platform with a transactional email API (idempotency keys, scheduling and cancel included) and AI-designed marketing campaigns in the same account. The idempotency docs cover the exact behaviour used above. If you've hit a duplicate-send bug with an agent, I'd like to hear how it happened in the comments.

title: I Built an Interactive Playground for Understanding AI Agent Harnesses
description:
When we talk about AI agents, we usually focus on the model, prompts, and tool calls. But there's a lot more happening behind the scenes.

Context engineering, memory, guardrails, policies, approvals, execution, tracing, evaluations, and releases are all part of building an agent system. Yet these pieces are rarely explored together in a way that's easy to understand.

I wanted to see these pieces work, not just read about them.

So I built Harnesswalk, an open-source, interactive environment for exploring how an AI agent harness works, one node at a time.

What is Harnesswalk?

Think of it as a visual playground for understanding AI agent engineering.

Instead of looking at a static architecture diagram, you can interact with an agent's execution flow and see what happens at each stage.

Some things you can explore:

  • Step-by-step execution: Follow a request as it travels through the harness, one node at a time.
  • Prompt inspection: See the exact prompt being prepared before a model call.
  • Component inspection: Explore the code and configuration behind individual nodes.
  • Human-in-the-loop: Approve or reject tool actions before execution.
  • Event replay: Go back and inspect what happened during an execution.
  • Experimentation: Disable individual nodes and observe how the system behaves without them.

The idea is to make the architecture tangible rather than treating the agent as a black box.

A note on scope

Harnesswalk currently models a governed assistant with policies, approvals, audit, memory, and a release gate.

It's a teaching model, not a debugger for existing agents or a coding-agent harness with shell access and subagents.

It's still evolving, and there are plenty of things I'd like to improve. But the webapp is already available, runs in the browser without installation, and supports an offline mode using a scripted model.

What's next?

I'm interested in exploring how this could evolve beyond an interactive learning environment.

Some directions I'm considering include multimodal agent workflows, more extensible component contracts, and eventually a registry where developers can add or replace capabilities such as RAG, memory implementations, model providers, and evaluation workflows.

For now, I'm focusing on making the existing experience useful and learning from people building agentic systems.

Give it a try

🌐 Explore the Harnesswalk webapp

📦 Source code on GitHub

📝 A deeper look at the architecture

It's open source under the Apache-2.0 license.

I'd love to hear from other developers:

What's missing from the architecture? Which components would you add, replace, or remove? And how would you approach making an agent harness more observable and easier to understand?

Feedback, ideas, and contributions are welcome!

title: I Said Screens Would Not Reach the Windows Hub. I Was Wrong
description:
Anton wants Screens 5 on every machine in the fleet: Mac Studio, Mac Pro and the hub. It is an app for controlling a computer remotely from an iPhone. The phone client is already installed. What is left is the server side on the computers, the configuration, and a check that connecting from the phone actually works.

Three things the recall says before the first install.

The hub runs Windows, and that is not a blocker, it is a different installer. Our node registry lists six machines: the Hetzner anchor on Linux, the hub and two more nodes on Windows, two MacBooks on macOS. Screens is an Apple-side client, so the instinct is that the hub is out of reach. It is not: Screens Connect runs on Windows and installs a VNC server (TightVNC) itself as part of setup, and the option can be deselected if a VNC server is already present. It also configures the Windows firewall.

⚠️ I got this wrong when the brief was first written. I flagged "the hub is on Windows, Screens has no server side for it" as a factual risk. That was false: the server side exists, it just arrives as Screens Connect rather than as the same package the Macs get. Correcting it here rather than leaving it in the file.

Second, three limits of the protocol that will shape what this is useful for. Screens does not transmit sound, because VNC does not carry audio. Clipboard sharing on Windows is limited to text and URLs, so no files and no images through the clipboard. And a secure connection on Windows needs a separate SSH server, which is not part of the Screens Connect install.

So the honest description of what he is building is a hands-on remote screen for interactive work, not a way to monitor long runs with sound or to move files between phone and machine. For a fleet where most work is sessions and logs, that is still the right tool; it just will not replace the shell.

Third, and this is the part worth deciding before installing anything: we already have two remote paths, and a third one was ordered six days ago. Cross-machine access in the fleet is closed by Tailscale plus ssh, which is why a deep research piece on remote-desktop tooling (AnyDesk, RustDesk, RDP, VNC) was parked with the verdict that a remote-desktop layer was not needed. Then on 29 October a new research order went out on exactly this question, for the Europe-to-US case where AnyDesk was lagging badly.

Which means Screens is the third approach to one problem, and the three do not overlap cleanly: Tailscale plus ssh is the machine-to-machine path and has no screen; AnyDesk is the human-at-a-desktop path and is the one being audited for latency; Screens is the phone-in-hand path and is the only one of the three that answers "I am away from the keyboard".

⚠️ One more thing the registry says and the brief does not: Mac Studio and Mac Pro are not in the node registry. The Studio was bought on 27 October and never entered; six nodes are listed and neither of those two is among them. So "every machine in the fleet" currently means two machines that the fleet does not formally know about, plus a hub that does. Installing a remote-control server on a machine the registry cannot see is how a node ends up outside every watchdog we have.

And one known local conflict, since it costs an evening when it bites. Avast interferes with Screens Connect and needs an explicit exception. We have already paid for this class of problem once on this very node: ExpressVPN silently broke Tailscale by cutting external DNS resolvers, and the cure was split tunnelling with the daemon excluded by hand. Security software that rewrites network paths is the first suspect when a remote connection works locally and dies from outside.

So the order of work, narrower than "install and configure": enter Mac Studio and Mac Pro into the node registry first, so whatever gets installed is visible to the fleet; install Screens Connect on the hub knowing it brings TightVNC with it; add the firewall and antivirus exceptions deliberately rather than after the first failure; decide whether the SSH server goes up on Windows for a secured connection or whether the Tailscale path already covers it; and test from the phone from outside the home network, because that is the only test that distinguishes a working setup from a working LAN.

The full story, in two versions:
📖 For humans, the longread: https://github.com/tonydzi/clawrush/blob/main/longreads/20261103.md
🤖 For machines, the devlog: https://github.com/tonydzi/clawrush/blob/main/devlog/20261103.md. Just hand this link to your coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor) and it will figure everything out: it is written for machines.

🔗 All our channels and contacts in one place: https://linktr.ee/PaloAltoAI

Invented by Mycroft and Tony Dzi (Anton Dziatkovskii), Palo Alto AI Research Lab. Proudly made in Silicon Valley.

title: A human-gated incident agent in a Switch room: a first-timer walkthrough
description:
If you have ever been on call, you know the shape of the problem. A watchdog alert fires at 2 AM, and the hardest question is not "what happened?" but "what is safe to do about it right now?". Autonomous agents make that question scarier, not easier — an LLM with write access to your cluster at 2 AM is not a workflow, it is a liability.

For the Flip the Switch Hackathon we built Graveyard Foreman: an incident triage agent that joins the team chat through Switch, classifies incoming reports, proposes exactly one safe next action, and refuses to do anything consequential until a human replies approve. This post walks through what we built, how we set it up with Switch, and what we learned — written for someone who has never used Switch before.

What Switch actually is (30 seconds)

Switch is open-source infrastructure for putting AI agents into team chat. Each channel becomes a room, and agents join rooms like teammates — with their own name, avatar, and instructions. The agent protocol is deliberately small: server-sent events in, HTTP out. Anything that speaks it can join a room, whatever it was built with.

Switch ships no agents and no models. You bring your own — Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, or a custom one like ours — and Switch connects it to Slack, Microsoft Teams, Discord, Telegram, or Mattermost. Switch Console, the desktop app, runs your agents, starts a local server in Docker, and bridges your chat apps.

What we built

Graveyard Foreman is a triage agent for small ops teams that receive noisy watchdog alerts after hours. An operator posts an incident in the room. The Foreman then:

  1. restates the report in one line,
  2. classifies it P0 / P1 / P2 and shows the evidence it used,
  3. proposes exactly one safe next action — never a menu, never two — and waits.

Nothing consequential executes until a human replies approve. A reject puts the action on HOLD with no side effect. Every report, proposal, decision, and receipt stays in the room, so the channel itself becomes the audit trail:

Piotr · human     payments-api: all users cannot pay. 100% 5xx after deploy 1842 at 09:42Z.

Foreman · agent   P0. Evidence: 100% 5xx on /v1/charge, started 09:42Z, one deploy at 09:40Z.
                  Proposed action: freeze deploys and page on-call. Approval required.

Piotr · human     approve

Foreman · agent   Executed. Deploys frozen, on-call paged. Receipt #r-882 written to this room.

The rejected path matters as much as the happy one. A second exchange in our demo ends with reject — the Foreman replies Action on HOLD. No changes made. and the room keeps the full record of a decision not to act, which is exactly the thing that is impossible to reconstruct from shell history.

Setup, step by step (what we actually did)

  1. Start Switch Console. It runs a local server in Docker. For the chat side we used the Mattermost instance bundled with Switch — which means the entire demo runs without a company workspace, without asking anyone for admin access, and without touching production Slack.
  2. Create the room. One channel on the bridge: #graveyard-foreman.
  3. Import the room template. switch-room.yaml in the repo declares the agent (name, description, addressing, instructions) and the room (name, bridge, agents, users). The YAML deliberately leaves provider names and credentials as placeholders — no secrets in a public repo.
  4. Point the provider at your agent. The template is written for Codex or Claude Code in production. For the recorded demo we went one step more boring: a pure-Python state machine (foreman.py), so the run is deterministic, reproducible, and needs no API key at all.
  5. Post the incident. Paste the report from demo/CHAT-TRANSCRIPT.md into the room and watch the gate work: triage, proposal, approval, receipt.

The pattern worth stealing: the approval gate

The transferable idea is not the triage — it is the discipline around the moment of action:

  • One action per proposal. A single recommendation forces prioritization and keeps the human decision simple.
  • An explicit approve/reject vocabulary. No "sure, go ahead" ambiguity; the agent only recognizes the exact words.
  • A receipt written back to the room. If the action does not leave a note in the same channel it was approved in, you will not find it at 9 AM.
  • Reject means HOLD, not failure. The agent must be able to hear "no" without breaking the workflow.

This is what makes the room metaphor more than cosmetic: report, decision, and receipt live where the team already talks, instead of being split across a private bot DM and an opaque automation log.

What we learned

  • The room is the unit of work. Agents showing up as members with roles and instructions — rather than opaque side-channel bots — is what convinced the teammate in our demo that the transcript is the audit trail.
  • The bundled Mattermost is quietly the best onboarding feature. Building and recording a realistic demo without asking anyone for workspace access removes the single biggest friction in agent-at-work experiments.
  • The protocol is small enough to be boring, in the best way. A ~200-line deterministic Python agent could join a room with no framework lock-in. That is the test of an open protocol.

What we would want next from Switch: a first-class approval-gate primitive — a room-level object for actions that require human sign-off, with built-in approve/reject and a receipt — so every team does not reinvent this pattern in prompt text; and room templates that ship one command away from the agent's first reply, to shorten the gap between importing a room and seeing it work.

Run it yourself (two minutes) 

git clone https://github.com/Schultzenator/HCTN
cd HCTN/flip-the-switch-2026
python3 foreman.py demo
python3 -m unittest -v

The demo plays the full safety-critical sequence — human report, triage, proposed action, human approval, action receipt — plus a rejected action and an incomplete report. The engine refuses to execute in both failure cases, and the tests pin that behavior down.

Switch's pitch for this hackathon was "turn your solo agent into a teammate". After a weekend of dogfooding it, our honest summary: the room metaphor is what makes human-in-the-loop automation feel safe enough to actually deploy — and the moment you stop letting the agent improvise consequential actions is the moment your teammates stop muting it.

title: Fal raises $1.3B at a $16B valuation, led by Bessemer
description:
AI infrastructure company fal has closed a $1.3 billion Series F round, as reported by Tech.eu. Bessemer Venture Partners led the round, with NVIDIA, Sound Ventures, HOF Capital and T. Rowe Price also taking part.

The numbers

Fal announced the Series F together with a $350 million Series E that Sequoia Capital led in April. The two rounds add up to $1.65 billion. Citing Bloomberg, Tech.eu says the new round values the company at $16 billion, twice the $8 billion valuation from April. Fal was founded in 2021 by Burkay Gür and Görkem Yurtseven.

What fal does

The company builds infrastructure for generative media. Businesses use it to run image, video and audio models at scale and to fit generative AI into the production and creative workflows they already have. The source names entertainment, advertising, e-commerce, gaming and marketing as the main customer industries.

During 2026, fal has worked on the quality and speed of generative media models using post-training techniques. It also continues to develop its own models next to those supplied by partners.

Where the money goes

According to the source, the funding will pay for expanding fal's inference infrastructure and team, and for further work on its generative media technology. The company plans to put money into research and test new approaches to AI-assisted content creation through 2027.

What the source does not say

The article gives no new product, model, price or plan, and no customer terms. Any effect on the cost or speed of generating media for fal's users is not stated and remains unconfirmed.

Why it is on our radar

Generative media is moving from experiments to a layer that companies build production work on, and the investor list in this round points to continued capital for the compute underneath it. For a business that buys such capacity through an API, the practical questions concern vendor dependence and portability rather than the valuation itself.
